claim: The EM data set consisted of 1917 thin (<50 nm) sections cut in the frontal plane.
source: The series consisted of 1917 thin (<50 nm) sections cut in the frontal plane.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript describing the EM data collection methodology.

claim: Each section was acquired at 4 × 4 nm2/pixel resolution.
source: Each section was acquired at 4 × 4 nm2/pixel, amounting to 4 million camera images and 50 TB of raw data.
evidence: Direct statement describing the imaging resolution.

claim: The EM imaging amounted to 4 million camera images and 50 TB of raw data.
source: Each section was acquired at 4 × 4 nm2/pixel, amounting to 4 million camera images and 50 TB of raw data.
evidence: Direct statement describing the data volume.

claim: Sections were imaged to capture both sides of the brain (up to 400 × 750 µm2), including both right and left copies of the antennal lobe.
source: Sections were imaged to capture both sides of the brain (up to 400 × 750 µm2), including both right and left copies of the antennal lobe.
evidence: Direct statement describing the imaging coverage.

claim: 53 ORNs innervated DM6, with 27 axons coming from the left antenna and 26 from the right.
source: In total, 53 ORNs innervated DM6, with 27 axons coming from the left antenna and 26 from the right.
evidence: Direct statement from reconstruction data.

claim: One right ORN and one left ORN projected only ipsilaterally.
source: However, we found that one right ORN and one left ORN projected only ipsilaterally.
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data.

claim: Each glomerulus contained the axons of 52 ORNs.
source: Therefore, each glomerulus contained the axons of 52 ORNs.
evidence: Inference from the observation that 53 ORNs innervated DM6 but two projected only ipsilaterally.

claim: Three 'sister' PNs were found on the left side of the brain and two on the right.
source: Interestingly, we found three 'sister' PNs on the left side the brain and two on the right.
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data.

claim: The number of DM6 PNs is often different on the two sides of the brain, although with no consistent trend for left PNs to outnumber right PNs, or vice versa.
source: This is not an unusual occurrence: we found that the number of DM6 PNs is often different on the two sides of the brain, although with no consistent trend for left PNs to outnumber right PNs, or vice versa (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observation from photoactivation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Variations in neuron number appear to be a general phenomenon.
source: Thus, variations in neuron number appear to be general phenomenon.
evidence: Inference from observations of variable PN counts.

claim: At least some of the variability in PN counts is due to true variation in PN counts, and is not merely due to variations in Gal4 expression patterns.
source: Our EM reconstruction implies that at least some of this variability is due to true variation in PN counts, and is not merely due to variations in Gal4 expression patterns.
evidence: Inference from EM reconstruction data compared to Gal4 labeling data.

claim: The percentage of orphans (fragments that could not be connected to any neuron) was 6.8 ± 1.5% overall.
source: Overall, the percentage of orphans was relatively small (6.8 ± 1.5%, mean ± SEM).
evidence: Direct measurement from reconstruction data.

claim: The percentage of orphans was lower for the left glomerulus (4.4 ± 0.8%) than for the right glomerulus (10.4 ± 0.4%).
source: This value was lower for the left glomerulus (4.4 ± 0.8%) than for the right glomerulus (10.4 ± 0.4%).
evidence: Direct measurement from reconstruction data.

claim: ORNs delivered about one-third of their synaptic output to PNs.
source: Beginning with ORN output synapses, we found that ORNs delivered about one-third of their synaptic output to PNs (Figure 1E).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Most of the remainder of ORN synaptic output was delivered to multiglomerular neurons.
source: Most of the remainder was delivered to multiglomerular neurons (Figure 1E).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: DM6 ORN axons received most of their synaptic input from multiglomerular neurons.
source: We found that DM6 ORN axons received most of their synaptic input from multiglomerular neurons (Figure 1E).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: About a third of synapses onto ORN axon terminals originated from PNs and ORNs.
source: About a third of synapses onto ORN axon terminals originated from PNs and ORNs.
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data.

claim: PNs received most of their input (~75%) from ORNs.
source: Turning to the PN's perspective, we found that PNs received most of their input (~75%) from ORNs, as expected (Figure 1F).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PNs received a sizeable input (~20%) from multiglomerular neurons.
source: PNs also received a sizeable input (~20%) from multiglomerular neurons.
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data.

claim: PNs devoted almost all of their output synapses (~90%) to multiglomerular neurons.
source: Within the DM6 glomerulus, we observed that PNs devoted almost all of their output synapses (~90%) to multiglomerular neurons (Figure 1F).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PNs devoted a small part of their output to ORN axon terminals.
source: PNs devoted a small part of their output to ORN axon terminals.
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data.

claim: Every PN made connections with all the other PNs in the same glomerulus.
source: Finally, every PN also made connections with all the other PNs in the same glomerulus, consistent with electrophysiological evidence for reciprocal synaptic interactions between sister DM6 PNs (Kazama and Wilson, 2009).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data, consistent with prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: Unitary ORN→PN connections were composed of about 23 synapses on average.
source: On average, unitary ORN→PN connections were composed of about 23 synapses (Figure 1G).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: An isolated ORN spike typically depolarizes a PN by about 5 mV.
source: An isolated ORN spike typically depolarizes a PN by about 5 mV, and the size of this unitary excitatory postsynaptic potential (uEPSP) is highly reliable from trial to trial.
evidence: Reference to prior physiological studies.

claim: The average number of synapses per unitary ORN→PN connection is similar to that predicted by quantal analysis in whole-cell recordings.
source: The average number of synapses that we detected per unitary ORN→PN connection is similar to that predicted by quantal analysis in whole-cell recordings (Kazama and Wilson, 2008) and also by light microscopy methods (Mosca and Luo, 2014).
evidence: Comparison with prior electrophysiological and light microscopy studies.

claim: Unitary PN→PN connections were composed of about 11 synapses on average.
source: Unitary PN→PN connections were composed of about 11 synapses, on average (Figure 1G).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: ORN→ORN connections and PN→ORN connections typically consisted of just one or two synapses.
source: ORN→ORN connections and PN→ORN connections typically consisted of just one or two synapses.
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data.

claim: Each ORN presynaptic element (T-bar) is presynaptic to multiple postsynaptic profiles, often one PN profile and one or two non-PN profiles.
source: It should be noted that each ORN presynaptic element (i.e., each 'T-bar') is presynaptic to multiple postsynaptic profiles, often one PN profile and one or two non-PN profiles (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The size of a T-bar was strongly correlated with the number of postsynaptic profiles.
source: The size of a T-bar was strongly correlated with the number of postsynaptic profiles; it was also significantly (though weakly) correlated with the surface area of the postsynaptic contacts (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Direct observation from measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The total dendritic path length was larger for individual PNs on the right as compared to individual PNs on the left.
source: The first thing we noticed was that the total dendritic path length was larger for individual PNs on the right as compared to individual PNs on the left (Figure 2A), possibly because right PNs had fewer sister cells, and so their dendrites had more space to fill.
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The total number of ORN→PN synapses was similar in the left and right glomerulus.
source: Notably, the total number of ORN→PN synapses was similar in the left and right glomerulus (Figure 2B).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The number of ORN synapses received by an individual PN was 53% higher on the right than on the left.
source: However, because there were three left PNs but only two right PNs, the number of ORN synapses received by an individual PN was 53% higher on the right than on the left.
evidence: Calculation from reconstruction data.

claim: ORN→PN synapse density was similar in left and right PNs.
source: Because PNs on the right also had larger dendrites, this resulted in a similar ORN→PN synapse density in left and right PNs (Figure 2C).
evidence: Calculation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The number of multiglomerular neuron synapses received by an individual PN was higher on the right than on the left.
source: Finally, the number of multiglomerular neuron synapses received by an individual PN was also higher on the right than on the left (Figure 2D), and individual PNs on the right formed more presynaptic contacts than did individual PNs on the left (Figure 2E).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: Individual PNs on the right formed more presynaptic contacts than did individual PNs on the left.
source: Finally, the number of multiglomerular neuron synapses received by an individual PN was also higher on the right than on the left (Figure 2D), and individual PNs on the right formed more presynaptic contacts than did individual PNs on the left (Figure 2E).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The simulated somatic uEPSP amplitudes were almost identical in right and left PNs.
source: Surprisingly, the simulated somatic uEPSP amplitudes were almost identical in right and left PNs (Figure 3C).
evidence: Result from compartmental modeling shown in Figure 3C.

claim: mEPSPs measured at the soma were much smaller in right PNs than in left PNs.
source: When we measured mEPSPs at the soma, they were much smaller in right PNs than in left PNs (Figure 3D).
evidence: Result from compartmental modeling shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The difference in mEPSP amplitude appeared when measured in the dendrite at the site of the synapse itself, reflecting a lower dendritic input resistance in right PNs.
source: The difference in mEPSP amplitude also appeared when we measured each mEPSP in the dendrite, at the site of the synapse itself (Figure 3E), reflecting a lower dendritic input resistance in right PNs (Figure 3F).
evidence: Result from compartmental modeling shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: In right PNs, mEPSPs decayed significantly more as they propagated from the dendrite to the cell body.
source: Moreover, in right PNs, mEPSPs also decayed significantly more as they propagated from the dendrite to the cell body (Figure 3G), reflecting a longer average path length from synapse to cell body (Figure 2A).
evidence: Result from compartmental modeling shown in Figure 3G, related to anatomical measurements in Figure 2A.

claim: Right and left PNs have uniform average voltage responses to ORN spikes, in spite of their marked differences in dendrite size and synapse number.
source: In summary, we find that right and left PNs have uniform average voltage responses to ORN spikes, in spite of their marked differences in dendrite size and synapse number.
evidence: Summary of compartmental modeling results.

claim: The measured differences in synapse number precisely counterbalance the measured differences in dendrite size.
source: Whatever the mechanism that creates this compensatory effect, the key point is that the measured differences in synapse number precisely counterbalance the measured differences in dendrite size.
evidence: Inference from compartmental modeling results.

claim: Drosophila can lateralize odors by comparing ORN spike trains arising from the right and left antennae.
source: Drosophila can lateralize odors by comparing ORN spike trains arising from the right and left antennae.
evidence: Reference to prior behavioral studies.

claim: In response to a laterally asymmetric odor stimulus, flies will tend to turn toward the antenna that is stimulated more strongly.
source: In response to a laterally asymmetric odor stimulus, flies will tend to turn toward the antenna that is stimulated more strongly (Figure 4A) (Borst, 1983; Gaudry et al., 2013).
evidence: Reference to prior behavioral studies shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Unitary ORN→PN connections are 30–40% stronger on the side of the brain ipsilateral to the ORN's cell body.
source: Electrophysiological recordings have shown that unitary ORN→PN connections are 30–40% stronger on the side of the brain ipsilateral to the ORN's cell body (Gaudry et al., 2013).
evidence: Reference to prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: PNs received more input synapses from ipsilateral ORNs than from contralateral ORNs.
source: Indeed, we found that PNs received more input synapses from ipsilateral ORNs than from contralateral ORNs (Figure 4C).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Compartmental models predicted that ipsilateral uEPSPs are 27% stronger than contralateral uEPSPs, on average.
source: Accordingly, our compartmental models predicted that ipsilateral uEPSPs are 27% stronger than contralateral uEPSPs, on average (Figure 4D).
evidence: Result from compartmental modeling shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There was no systematic ipsi-contra difference in the placement of synapses onto the PN's dendritic tree, as judged by the mean mEPSP amplitude at the PN soma.
source: There was no systematic ipsi-contra difference in the placement of synapses onto the PN's dendritic tree, as judged by the mean mEPSP amplitude at the PN soma (Figure 4E).
evidence: Result from compartmental modeling shown in Figure 4E.

claim: There was no significant difference in the total path length of ipsi- and contralateral ORN axons within the boundaries of glomerulus DM6.
source: There was also no significant difference in the total path length of ipsi- and contralateral ORN axons within the boundaries of glomerulus DM6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The difference in the electrophysiological properties of ipsi- and contralateral connections is largely explained by a single structural difference: PNs receive more synapses from ipsilateral than from contralateral ORNs.
source: In short, we find that the difference in the electrophysiological properties of ipsi- and contralateral connections is largely explained by a single structural difference: PNs receive more synapses from ipsilateral than from contralateral ORNs.
evidence: Summary of reconstruction and modeling results.

claim: The ipsi-contra asymmetry is not perfectly precise at the level of single synaptic connections: some ipsi connections are weaker than contra connections onto the same PN.
source: The ipsi-contra asymmetry is not perfectly precise at the level of single synaptic connections: some ipsi connections are weaker than contra connections onto the same PN (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The ipsi-contra difference is sufficiently precise to permit PNs to prefer ipsilateral stimuli over contralateral stimuli, provided that the stimuli are sufficiently strong.
source: However, as we will show below, this difference is sufficiently precise to permit PNs to prefer ipsilateral stimuli over contralateral stimuli, provided that the stimuli are sufficiently strong.
evidence: Inference from modeling results presented later in the manuscript.

claim: The main source of variation among ORN→PN connections was the number of synapses per connection.
source: The main source of variation was the number of synapses per connection.
evidence: Inference from reconstruction data analysis.

claim: The number of synapses per connection varied over a wide range: a typical PN received only 10 synapses from one ipsilateral ORN, but 36 synapses from another ipsilateral ORN.
source: This number varied over a wide range: for example, a typical PN received only 10 synapses from one ipsilateral ORN, but 36 synapses from another ipsilateral ORN (left PN1, Figure 5B).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The number of synapses per connection was correlated with the physical proximity of ORN axons and PN dendrites.
source: The number of synapses per connection was correlated with the physical proximity of ORN axons and PN dendrites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting the number of synapses connecting each ORN-PN pair simply scales with the amount of axon-dendrite contact.
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Across all connections, the coefficient of variation (CV) in the percentage contribution of each ORN to a PN pool of ORN synapses was 0.31.
source: Across all connections, the coefficient of variation (CV) in this value was 0.31, consistent with previous estimates based on optical methods (Mosca and Luo, 2014).
evidence: Calculation from reconstruction data, consistent with prior optical studies.

claim: There was little variability among connections in the mean amplitude of a simulated mEPSP at the soma of the compartmental models.
source: By comparison, there was little variability among connections in the mean amplitude of a simulated mEPSP at the soma of the compartmental models (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Result from compartmental modeling shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Summation efficacy was relatively consistent across ORN→PN connections.
source: Summation efficacy was also relatively consistent across ORN→PN connections (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Result from compartmental modeling shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: Most connections had summation efficacies near 0.9, indicating weakly sublinear summation.
source: Most connections had summation efficacies near 0.9, indicating weakly sublinear summation.
evidence: Result from compartmental modeling.

claim: The major source of variation among ORN→PN connections is simply the number of synapses per connection.
source: In short, the major source of variation among ORN→PN connections is simply the number of synapses per connection.
evidence: Summary of reconstruction and modeling results.

claim: The variation in synapse number should produce a relatively large range in uEPSP amplitudes.
source: Our models indicate that this source of variation should produce a relatively large range in uEPSP amplitudes (Figure 5H and Figure 3B).
evidence: Result from compartmental modeling shown in Figure 5H and Figure 3B.

claim: Different ORNs in the same antenna should have quite different effects on the PN membrane potential, with the strongest ORNs outweighing the weakest ORNs by almost 10-fold.
source: Different ORNs in the same antenna should have quite different effects on the PN membrane potential, with the strongest ORNs outweighing the weakest ORNs by almost 10-fold.
evidence: Inference from compartmental modeling results.

claim: PNs do not assign equal weight to ORNs from the same antenna.
source: Thus, it seems that PNs do not assign equal weight to ORNs from the same antenna.
evidence: Inference from reconstruction and modeling results.

claim: The PN response is likely to be dominated by only a fraction of the ORN population.
source: Rather, the PN response is likely to be dominated by only a fraction of the ORN population.
evidence: Inference from reconstruction and modeling results.

claim: ORN spikes virtually always produce synchronous synaptic events in all ipsi- and contralateral target PNs.
source: Paired electrophysiological recordings from sister PNs show that ORN spikes virtually always produce synchronous synaptic events in all ipsi- and contralateral target PNs (Kazama and Wilson, 2009).
evidence: Reference to prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: All sister PNs experience the same ORN spike trains, even if they are located on opposite sides of the brain.
source: In essence, all sister PNs experience the same ORN spike trains, even if they are located on opposite sides of the brain.
evidence: Inference from prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: 7 of the 8 ipsilateral comparisons produced a significant correlation in connection strength (normalized synapse counts) between PNs on the same side.
source: Specifically, 7 of the 8 ipsilateral comparisons produced a significant correlation (Pearson's r ranged from 0.44 to 0.78, p<0.05; the exception is left PN2 and left PN3, where r = 0.36, p=0.07).
evidence: Statistical analysis of reconstruction data.

claim: There was no correlation in connection strength (normalized synapse counts) between right and left PNs.
source: However, we found no correlation between right and left PNs (Figure 6B–D; for the 12 contralateral comparisons r ranged from −0.21 to 0.34, p>0.09)
evidence: Statistical analysis of reconstruction data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: The failure to find correlations among all PNs argues that ORN→PN connection strengths are not optimized to match some feature of each ORN's spiking behavior.
source: The failure to find correlations among all PNs argues that ORN→PN connection strengths are not optimized to match some feature of each ORN's spiking behavior.
evidence: Inference from statistical analysis of reconstruction data.

claim: At least some of the variation in ORN→PN connections is due to 'connection noise' – that is, imprecision in synapse number specification.
source: Because we do not observe this sort of correlation, then it seems likely that at least some of the variation in ORN→PN connections is due to 'connection noise' – that is, imprecision in synapse number specification.
evidence: Inference from statistical analysis of reconstruction data.

claim: Connection noise should limit the accuracy of a PNs estimate of the stimulus based on incoming ORN spike trains.
source: This connection noise should limit the accuracy of a PNs estimate of the stimulus based on incoming ORN spike trains.
evidence: Inference from the observation of connection noise.

claim: At the perceptual threshold for odor detection, the olfactory system must be able to detect an odor based on an increase in ORN spikes above the expected number of spontaneous spikes.
source: It is important to note that all ORNs fire spontaneously even in the absence of odor (de Bruyne et al., 2001). Thus, at the perceptual threshold for odor detection, the olfactory system must be able to detect an odor based on an increase in ORN spikes above the expected number of spontaneous spikes.
evidence: Reference to prior studies and logical inference.

claim: During a 200 ms counting window, in one antenna, the entire DM6 ORN population fires an average of 12 spontaneous spikes in the absence of an odor.
source: During this counting window, in one antenna, the entire DM6 ORN population fires an average of 12 spontaneous spikes in the absence of an odor (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Calculation from electrophysiological measurements described in Materials and methods.

claim: The normal variation in the structure of ORN→PN connections can impair the ability of PNs to transmit information about ORN spike counts.
source: This simulation shows that the normal variation in the structure of ORN→PN connections can impair the ability of PNs to transmit information about ORN spike counts.
evidence: Result from classifier simulations.

claim: The normal imprecision in the structure of ORN→PN connections can impair the ability of PNs to transmit information about right-left differences in ORN spike counts.
source: This simulation shows that the normal imprecision in the structure of ORN→PN connections can impair the ability of PNs to transmit information about right-left differences in ORN spike counts, particularly because connection noise is correlated within each half of the brain, but uncorrelated across the midline.
evidence: Result from classifier simulations.

claim: The number of synapses per connection was strongly correlated with the strength of ORN→PN connections.
source: Notably, we found that the number of synapses per connection was strongly correlated with the strength of ORN→PN connections.
evidence: Summary of reconstruction and modeling results.

claim: Ipsilateral connections contain 35% more synapses per connection than contralateral connections.
source: Here, we discovered that ipsilateral connections contain 35% more synapses per connection (Figure 4C).
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There is not a sizeable ipsi-contra difference in synaptic conductance.
source: This result argues that the difference in the number of synapses per connection is the main difference between ipsi and contra connections. By extension, we can infer that there is not a sizeable ipsi-contra difference in synaptic conductance.
evidence: Inference from the observation that synapse number explains the ipsi-contra difference in connection strength.

claim: From the perspective of an individual PN, there was little variation across ORN connections in the average strength of the synapses that comprised each connection.
source: Interestingly, from the perspective of an individual PN, there was little variation across ORN connections in the average strength of the synapses that comprised each connection (Figure 5E).
evidence: Result from compartmental modeling shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Dendritic filtering has an essentially uniform effect on all ORN→PN connections.
source: Thus, insofar as our models accurately represent the structure of each PN dendrite, it predicts that dendritic filtering has an essentially uniform effect on all ORN→PN connections.
evidence: Inference from compartmental modeling results.

claim: Each connection is composed of many quasi-random 'samples' of dendritic filtering properties, and so the average effect of dendritic filtering is similar across connections.
source: In essence, each connection is composed of many quasi-random 'samples' of dendritic filtering properties, and so the average effect of dendritic filtering is similar across connections.
evidence: Inference from compartmental modeling results.

claim: The number of neurons in Drosophila neural networks is variable.
source: Although Drosophila neural networks are sometimes regarded as highly stereotyped, the number of neurons in such a network is actually variable.
evidence: Reference to prior studies and current observations.

claim: In the optic lobe, in 3 of 7 networks analyzed, one cell that ought to be present was in fact missing.
source: In the optic lobe, a recent EM study analyzed 7 repetitions of a modular neural network that normally contains 23 uniquely identifiable cells. In 3 of the 7 networks, one cell that ought to be present was in fact missing (Takemura et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to prior EM study.

claim: When a cell is missing in the optic lobe, there can be compensatory changes in wiring.
source: In the case of one missing cell, a homologous cell in a neighboring column sent an extra branch into the vacated space, where it received synapses from the normal presynaptic partners of the missing cell. Thus, when a cell is missing, there can be compensatory changes in wiring.
evidence: Reference to prior EM study.

claim: Variations in antennal lobe PN numbers have been inferred previously based on Gal4 expression patterns.
source: Variations in antennal lobe PN numbers have been inferred previously based on Gal4 expression patterns (Grabe et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2004).
evidence: Reference to prior studies.

claim: Based on Gal4 expression, there can be two, three, or four PNs in glomerulus DM6, with the 'typical' situation (three PNs) occurring only 67% of the time.
source: Indeed, based on Gal4 expression, we find that there can be two, three, or four PNs in glomerulus DM6, with the 'typical' situation (three PNs) occurring only 67% of the time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct observation from photoactivation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the glomerulus with fewer PNs, PN dendrites were larger, perhaps because they had more space to fill.
source: In the glomerulus with fewer PNs, we found that PN dendrites were larger, perhaps because they had more space to fill.
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data with speculative explanation.

claim: There was a compensatory increase in synapse numbers per PN in the glomerulus with fewer PNs, so that the total number of synapses per glomerulus was similar on the left and right.
source: Moreover, there was also a compensatory increase in synapse numbers per PN, so that the total number of synapses per glomerulus was similar on the left and right.
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data.

claim: In the glomerulus with only two PNs, the up-regulation in synapse number was neatly balanced by the increased size of PN dendrites.
source: Remarkably, in the glomerulus with only two PNs, the up-regulation in synapse number was neatly balanced by the increased size of PN dendrites.
evidence: Inference from compartmental modeling results.

claim: Increasing the size of a postsynaptic compartment produces a lower input resistance, and so each quantum of neurotransmitter produces a smaller depolarization.
source: As illustrated by classic work at the neuromuscular junction, increasing the size of a postsynaptic compartment produces a lower input resistance, and so each quantum of neurotransmitter produces a smaller depolarization (Katz and Thesleff, 1957).
evidence: Reference to classic neuromuscular junction studies.

claim: In each of the larger PNs, a presynaptic ORN spike should release more quanta than normal, but the postsynaptic voltage response to each quantum will be smaller.
source: In each of the larger PNs, a presynaptic ORN spike should release more quanta than normal, but the postsynaptic voltage response to each quantum will be smaller.
evidence: Inference from reconstruction and modeling results.

claim: Each PN has the same average response to an ORN spike despite differences in dendrite size and synapse number.
source: As a result, each PN has the same average response to an ORN spike.
evidence: Inference from compartmental modeling results.

claim: A decrease in presynaptic neurotransmitter release can elicit compensatory growth in postsynaptic dendrites in the larval ventral nerve cord.
source: For example, in the larval ventral nerve cord, a decrease in presynaptic neurotransmitter release can elicit compensatory growth in postsynaptic dendrites (Tripodi et al., 2008).
evidence: Reference to prior study.

claim: Cell-specific K+ channel overexpression to decrease a PN's input resistance results in a compensatory increase in unitary excitatory synaptic currents at ORN connections onto that PN.
source: A previous study used cell-specific K+ channel overexpression to decrease a PN's input resistance, and found a compensatory increase in unitary excitatory synaptic currents at ORN connections onto that PN (Kazama and Wilson, 2008).
evidence: Reference to prior study.

claim: PN dendrites can up-regulate synaptic currents to compensate for reduced dendritic excitability.
source: That result demonstrated that PN dendrites can up-regulate synaptic currents to compensate for reduced dendritic excitability.
evidence: Inference from prior study.

claim: When one PN failed to develop, the remaining PNs grew larger dendrites, and then synapse number increased to compensate for increased dendrite size.
source: Together, these findings suggest the following scenario. When one PN failed to develop, the remaining PNs grew larger dendrites, and then synapse number increased to compensate for increased dendrite size.
evidence: Inference from current and prior studies.

claim: PN dendrites form a glomerular map prior to the arrival of migrating ORN axon terminals.
source: This scenario is consistent with the well-described instructive role of PN dendrites in ORN axon development: PN dendrites form a glomerular map prior to the arrival of migrating ORN axon terminals (Jefferis et al., 2004).
evidence: Reference to prior study.

claim: At the developing vertebrate neuromuscular junction, the expansion of the postsynaptic cell seems to be primary, with the elaboration of the presynaptic arbor occurring in response.
source: At the developing vertebrate neuromuscular junction, the expansion of the postsynaptic cell seems to be primary, with the elaboration of the presynaptic arbor occurring in response (Balice-Gordon and Lichtman, 1990).
evidence: Reference to prior study.

claim: The number of synapses per ORN→PN connection was quite variable.
source: We found that the number of synapses per ORN→PN connection was quite variable.
evidence: Direct observation from reconstruction data.

claim: ORN→PN connections gave rise to simulated uEPSP amplitudes ranging from 1.6 to 10 mV.
source: As a result, ORN→PN connections gave rise to simulated uEPSP amplitudes ranging from 1.6 to 10 mV (Figure 5H).
evidence: Result from compartmental modeling shown in Figure 5H.

claim: If all ORNs were functionally identical, the variation in synapse number would be non-optimal, because each PN's response would be dominated by only a fraction of its presynaptic ORN axons.
source: If all ORNs were functionally identical, this sort of variation would be non-optimal, because each PN's response would be dominated by only a fraction of its presynaptic ORN axons.
evidence: Logical inference from modeling results.

claim: Connection noise may be a factor limiting perceptual acuity.
source: Our simulations suggest that connection noise may be a factor limiting perceptual acuity.
evidence: Inference from classifier simulation results.

claim: In the medulla of the optic lobe, the CV of synapse number per connection ranges from 0.08 to 0.87.
source: In the medulla of the optic lobe, the CV of synapse number per connection ranges from 0.08 to 0.87 (computed across all connections of a given type; Takemura et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to prior EM study.

claim: Synapse number variations were correlated across sister PNs on the same side of the brain, even though they were uncorrelated on the opposite sides of the brain.
source: Intriguingly, we found that synapse number variations were correlated across sister PNs on the same side of the brain, even though they were uncorrelated on the opposite sides of the brain.
evidence: Statistical analysis of reconstruction data.

claim: Correlated developmental noise may be one reason why sister PNs on the same side of the brain display such high levels of correlated electrical noise.
source: This sort of correlated developmental noise may be one reason why sister PNs on the same side of the brain display such high levels of correlated electrical noise (Kazama and Wilson, 2009).
evidence: Inference from current observations and prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: Sister PNs on the same side of the brain are dominated by the same pool of ORNs.
source: As we show here, sister PNs on the same side of the brain are dominated by the same pool of ORNs.
evidence: Inference from reconstruction data.

claim: Sister PN spike timing correlations represent a functionally-relevant constraint on circuit function which can affect both the speed and accuracy of odor stimulus responses.
source: As a result, sister PN spike timing correlations represent a functionally-relevant constraint on circuit function which can affect both the speed and accuracy of odor stimulus responses (Jeanne and Wilson, 2015).
evidence: Reference to prior study.

claim: In the larval antennal lobe, there are 21 glomeruli, as compared to ~50 in the adult.
source: In the larval antennal lobe, there are 21 glomeruli, as compared to ~50 in the adult.
evidence: Reference to prior knowledge.

claim: Each glomerulus in the larva contains just one ORN axon and one uniglomerular PN dendrite.
source: Moreover, each glomerulus in the larva is relatively simple: it contains just one ORN axon and one uniglomerular PN dendrite.
evidence: Reference to prior knowledge.

claim: In the larva, the average ORN→PN connection contains ~70 synapses, whereas in the adult, it contains 23 synapses.
source: In the larva, the average ORN→PN connection contains ~70 synapses. whereas in the adult, it contains 23 synapses.
evidence: Comparison of larval connectome data with current adult data.

claim: The increased number of ORNs in the adult is partly compensated by a decrease in the number of synapses per connection.
source: Thus, the increased number of ORNs in the adult is partly compensated by a decrease in the number of synapses per connection.
evidence: Inference from comparison of larval and adult data.

claim: In the larva, almost all synapses onto ORNs arise from multiglomerular neurons.
source: In the larva, almost all synapses onto ORNs arise from multiglomerular neurons.
evidence: Reference to larval connectome data.

claim: In the adult, most synapses onto ORNs arise from multiglomerular neurons, but a substantial minority arise from PNs and ORNs.
source: In the adult, most synapses onto ORNs arise from multiglomerular neurons, but a substantial minority arise from PNs and ORNs.
evidence: Direct observation from current reconstruction data.

claim: The adult network may exert more complicated control of ORN neurotransmitter release compared to the larval network.
source: This suggests that the adult network may exert more complicated control of ORN neurotransmitter release.
evidence: Inference from comparison of larval and adult connectivity patterns.

claim: Systematic variations in synaptic connections are evidence of the brain's functional capacity to match a connection's strength to its required function.
source: From this perspective, systematic variations in synaptic connections are evidence of the brain's functional capacity – the capacity to match a connection's strength to its required function.
evidence: Conceptual interpretation of findings.

claim: Systematic variations in connection strength arise largely as a result of differences in the number of synapses per connection.
source: Our results indicate that systematic variations in connection strength arise largely as a result of differences in the number of synapses per connection.
evidence: Summary of reconstruction and modeling results.

claim: Systematic ipsi-contra differences can enable odor lateralization.
source: We show how systematic ipsi-contra differences can enable odor lateralization, while systematic correlations between synapse number and dendrite size can equalize the response of different PNs to an average ORN spike.
evidence: Summary of reconstruction and modeling results.

claim: Systematic correlations between synapse number and dendrite size can equalize the response of different PNs to an average ORN spike.
source: We show how systematic ipsi-contra differences can enable odor lateralization, while systematic correlations between synapse number and dendrite size can equalize the response of different PNs to an average ORN spike.
evidence: Summary of reconstruction and modeling results.

claim: Unsystematic wiring variations ('connection noise') must limit the capacity of every neural system.
source: On the other hand, unsystematic wiring variations ('connection noise') must limit the capacity of every neural system.
evidence: Conceptual interpretation of findings.

claim: Some imprecision in wiring can be balanced by homeostatic changes to other parameters, including synaptic parameters.
source: Some of this imprecision can be balanced by homeostatic changes to other parameters, including synaptic parameters (Prinz et al., 2004; Roffman et al., 2012).
evidence: Reference to prior studies.

claim: There exist residual non-optimal wiring variations that can impair neural computations.
source: Our findings provide insight into the mechanisms underlying such compensatory changes, but our results also argue for the existence of residual non-optimal wiring variations that can impair neural computations.
evidence: Summary of findings and their implications.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster is likely to be the next organism whose brain is fully mapped at the connectomic level.
source: Drosophila melanogaster is likely to be the next organism whose brain is fully mapped at the connectomic level.
evidence: Speculation about future of connectomics.
